definition: Clustering data into a tree of nested groups — agglomerative (bottom-up) or divisive (top-down) — yielding a dendrogram cut at the desired granularity.
details: Clustering data into a tree of nested groups — agglomerative (bottom-up) or divisive (top-down) — yielding a dendrogram cut at the desired granularity.

explainer.lead: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of nested groups, agglomerative (bottom-up) or divisive (top-down), producing a dendrogram you cut at the desired granularity. It matters because it gives clusters at multiple levels rather than one fixed partition.

tiers.eli5: It's like organizing people into a family tree of groups: start with everyone alone and keep merging the closest pairs, or start with everyone together and keep splitting.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers pick a distance metric and linkage criterion, then cut the dendrogram at the granularity they need. A pitfall is that agglomerative merging is greedy and never undone, so early merge mistakes persist.
tiers.paperLevel: Hierarchical clustering seeks to build a hierarchy of clusters. Agglomerative methods begin with each point as a cluster and repeatedly merge the two most similar clusters by a distance metric and linkage criterion until one cluster remains; divisive methods start with one cluster and recursively split it. Agglomerative methods are more common and efficient for small to medium datasets; divisive methods are less common.

explainer.example: With single linkage and Euclidean distance, each data point starts as its own cluster and the closest pairs are merged step by step until a single cluster remains, then the tree is cut where the desired number of groups appears.
